brief.intro: New to this project type? A district cooling plant is a centralised chiller plant that produces chilled water and pumps it through a buried underground pipe network to many separate buildings, instead of each building having its own chillers. The programme has two very different halves that must be coordinated: the plant itself (chillers, pumps, pipework and sometimes a thermal energy storage tank) and the distribution network — kilometres of insulated buried pipe reaching each connected building's energy transfer station. Long-lead chillers and large pumps, plus the sheer length of the underground network, are what drive the schedule, not the plant building's structure. Commissioning is two-stage: the plant is proven first as a standalone system, then the network is proven building by building as each energy transfer station is connected and brought online.

scope.name: Site & civil works
scope.desc: Plant building foundations, network trenching route, and road/utility crossings.

scope.name: Plant building structure
scope.desc: Chiller hall, pump hall and electrical rooms — the structural shell housing the plant.

scope.name: Chiller plant
scope.desc: Centrifugal or absorption chillers with primary & secondary chilled-water pumps.

scope.name: Thermal energy storage (TES)
scope.desc: Chilled-water storage tank with charge/discharge piping and controls, where included.

scope.name: Distribution network
scope.desc: Buried pre-insulated chilled-water supply and return pipework across the site or district.

scope.name: Energy transfer stations (ETS)
scope.desc: Building-side heat exchangers and metering connecting each customer to the network.

scope.name: Electrical & switchgear
scope.desc: MV/LV power distribution for chillers, pumps and plant auxiliaries.

scope.name: BMS / plant control
scope.desc: Chiller sequencing, pump staging, network pressure/flow control and the ETS interface.

scope.name: Testing & commissioning
scope.desc: Plant start-up, network hydraulic/pressure testing, TES charge/discharge proving and ETS connection commissioning.

must_get_right: Treat the plant and the distribution network as two schedules that must be integrated, not one — network length and the number of ETS connections often outlast the plant build.
Chillers and large pumps are long-lead and procurement-led — order early; their delivery gates plant start-up.
The network is commissioned building by building as each ETS is connected — sequence and prioritise connections against the customer occupancy programme, don't leave them all to the end.
Protect the two-stage commissioning (plant proving, then network/ETS proving) — a rushed plant proving shows up later as network-wide problems.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. The distribution network is modelled as repeatable pipe segments and ETS connections rather than one lump activity, so trenching production rate and connection sequencing are both visible in the logic.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Network trenching runs an extended calendar where road/utility crossings require traffic management or night work; plant MEP installation runs a standard shift; commissioning moves to a 7-day calendar toward plant energisation and network handover.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs chiller/TES procurement → plant structure → chiller set & pipework, in parallel with network trenching and pipe-laying → plant standalone proving → network hydraulic test → ETS connections staged against customer building occupancy → performance run. The plant and the network are effectively two coordinated critical paths, and the network is often the longer of the two.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Way-leaves and road-crossing permits are secured ahead of trenching; each customer building's readiness for ETS connection matches the network's arrival at that building; TES is included per the approved design; and chiller selection is frozen before plant civil works begin. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Road and utility crossings need traffic management and third-party approvals that can gate trenching progress; trenching production rate is a resource constraint across a long, linear network; chiller and TES heavy lifts need crane access into the plant building before roof closure.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: long-lead chiller/pipe slippage, way-leave or road-crossing permit delay, customer building readiness mismatch at ETS connection, and hydrostatic test failures on long pipe runs. Schedule contingency is held before the network hydrostatic test and before the first ETS connection rather than spread thinly across pipe segments.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones — plant proving, first ETS connection, full network commissioned) and Level 2 (summary by network zone) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead per pipe segment/ETS for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
